newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Headless meter mystery in Washington.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Headless meter mystery in Washington.

text.p: Someone is killing the parking meters of Washington.
Row upon row of meters in the U.S. capital stand headless, decapitated by unknown assailants who thereby deprive a near-bankrupt city of even the small change it sorely needs.

"It's an all-out war," city council member and possible candidate for mayor Harold Brazil declared of vandals wielding baseball bats, crowbars or hammers who have bashed more than 2,200 of the city's 15,777 meters. On one block of busy K Street, the city's most expensive office corridor, all 12 meters were missing one day last week.

At 25 cents to park for 15 minutes in most places, the city is losing well over $3 million in quarters each year, officials say. But far more is lost in fines for tickets, at $15 to $100 each, written by the District of Colombia's zealous parking enforcement squad.

Brazil suspects dark forces are behind the meter mayhem, perhaps aimed at the enforcement squad itself. "Our parking enforcement system is overzealous, punitive and greedy ... it's made people terribly mad," he said.

Brazil and fellow council members are searching for a way to cope, considering tougher penalties for vandalism, buying expensive vandal-defying meters or turning over the whole meter operation to a private contractor.

Police are at a loss to pinpoint blame. They think homeless people may be smashing the meters to snatch the coins or roaming gangs of teenage hoodlums may be getting their kicks from meter mauling. Or it could be angry suburbanites fed up with paying hefty fines when they miss feeding the meter monsters on time and get hit with tickets, which can be issued every hour a car remains in an expired meter spot.

But to be honest, police officials said, they are not certain about motives. There have been only a handful of arrests in the past two years and no one has gone to jail for the offence, which has spread throughout the city from President Bill Clinton's White House neigborhood to the poorest sections of Anacostia.
Even if they could catch someone in the act, police said, meter battering is merely a misdemeanor vandalism charge. In a city riddled with serious crime, meter murder is a low priority.
But for Willie Johnson, a long-time city mechanic whose small Department of Public Works workshop is cluttered with battered meter parts, it is a mystery worth solving.
"They bring in three or four a day, and we're just running out of parts to fix them back up for the streets. We're lucky to get one or two a day back up," he said.

"It's hard to say who is doing all this, whether it's one person or a gang or just individual types who don't want to pay," he said. "Basically, it's a misdemeanor anyway. So what if they get arrested? Nothing happens."
But it may be worth noting that Mayor Marion Barry's new $3.3 billion budget plan slashes spending across the board with one notable exception: he wants to hire 11 more parking enforcement agents.
